facts.t: The term came from South Africa, not India
facts.d: It emerged in post-apartheid constitutional discourse to describe a document written to dismantle an unjust social order rather than merely to organise government. Indian courts adopted the vocabulary only after 2010.

facts.t: A. K. Gopalan and Puttaswamy read the same words differently
facts.d: Article 21 was unchanged between 1950 and 2017. What changed was the interpretive method — from literal reading of personal liberty to a structural, purposive one that located privacy within it.

Untouchability was abolished in 1950 and the practice banned by statute. It continues — the standard illustration that constitutional text and judicial pronouncement cannot substitute for executive enforcement.

bank.q: The concept of transformative constitutionalism originated in the constitutional discourse of:
bank.e: South Africa, describing a constitution written to dismantle an unjust social order. Indian jurisprudence adopted it after 2010.

bank.q: Match List I (case) with List II (transformative outcome):
pairs: 1. Decriminalisation of adultery as discriminatory against women
2. Recognition of transgender persons as the third gender
bank.e: NALSA on gender recognition, Navtej on Section 377, Joseph Shine on adultery, and Puttaswamy on privacy.

bank.q: With reference to the judicial phases described, consider the following:
s: The 1950s to 1970s were marked by conservative, literal interpretation.
Kesavananda introduced structural and purposive interpretation.
The 1990s to 2010s are labelled the transformative jurisprudence phase.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The 1990s to 2010s are the judicial activism phase; transformative jurisprudence is dated from the 2010s onward.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT cited as a constitutional foundation of transformative constitutionalism?
bank.e: The amending power is not among the foundations listed — the four are the Preamble, Part III, Part IV and the remedial articles.

bank.as: Transformative constitutionalism treats the Constitution as a living document.
bank.rs: It is understood as a dynamic instrument for dismantling entrenched hierarchies rather than a static legal text.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — the interpretive premise on which the entire body of post-2010 jurisprudence rests.

bank.q: Consider the following policy translations of judicially recognised rights:
s: The Right to Education Act, 2009 under Article 21A.
The National Food Security Act, 2013 built on the judicially recognised right to food.
The POSH Act following the Vishaka guidelines.
bank.e: All three are correct — each converting a judicial recognition into statutory entitlement.

bank.q: All of the following are challenges to transformative constitutionalism EXCEPT:
o: Expanding judicial recognition of intersectional rights
bank.e: That is an achievement of the doctrine, not an obstacle to it.

bank.q: Which case is cited for secularism as basic structure within transformative jurisprudence?
bank.e: S. R. Bommai (1994), which also limited misuse of Article 356 and thereby strengthened federalism.

bank.q: With reference to caste and reservation jurisprudence, consider the following:
s: Indra Sawhney upheld OBC reservation with the creamy layer exclusion.
Jarnail Singh extended the creamy layer to SC and ST promotions.
Davinder Singh barred sub-categorisation within Scheduled Castes.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Davinder Singh (2024) permitted sub-categorisation rather than barring it.

bank.q: Which judgment first read the right to livelihood into Article 21?
bank.e: Olga Tellis (1985), holding livelihood intrinsic to the right to life.

bank.as: Real transformation requires more than judicial pronouncement.
bank.rs: Legislature, executive and civil society must implement constitutional ideals on the ground.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — the persistence of manual scavenging despite Article 17 is the standing illustration.
